# bit_set - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bit-set/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#description)Description

An implementation of a set using a bit vector as an underlying representation for holding unsigned numerical elements.

It should also be noted that the amount of storage necessary for holding a
set of objects is proportional to the maximum of the objects when viewed
as a `usize`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use bit_set::BitSet;
// It's a regular set
let mut s = BitSet::new();
s.insert(0);
s.insert(3);
s.insert(7);
s.remove(7);
if !s.contains(7) {
    println!("There is no 7");
}
// Can initialize from a `BitVec`
let other = BitSet::from_bytes(&[0b11010000]);
s.union_with(&other);
// Print 0, 1, 3 in some order
for x in s.iter() {
    println!("{}", x);
}
// Can convert back to a `BitVec`
let bv = s.into_bit_vec();
assert!(bv[3]);
```

- [BitSet](https://docs.rs/struct.BitSet.html)
- [Difference](https://docs.rs/struct.Difference.html)
- [Intersection](https://docs.rs/struct.Intersection.html)

- An iterator for `BitSet`.

- [Union](https://docs.rs/struct.Union.html)

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- Abstracts over a pile of bits (basically unsigned primitives)

# bit-set 0.10.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/bit-set/latest

## Usage

Add this to your Cargo.toml:

```
[]
 = "0.10"
```
Since Rust 2018, `extern crate` is no longer mandatory. If your edition is old (Rust 2015),
add this to your crate root:

```
extern crate bit_set;
```
If you want to use `serde`, enable it with the `serde` feature:

```
[]
 = {  = "0.10",  = ["serde"] }
```
If you want to use bit-set in a program that has `#![no_std]`, just drop default features:

```
[]
 = {  = "0.10",  = false }
```
If you want to use serde with the alloc crate instead of std, just use the `serde_no_std` feature:

```
[]
 = {  = "0.10",  = false,  = ["serde", "serde_no_std"] }
```
If you want [borsh-rs](https://github.com/near/borsh-rs) support, include it like this:

```
[]
 = {  = "0.10",  = ["borsh"] }
```
Other available serialization libraries can be enabled with the
[ miniserde](https://github.com/dtolnay/miniserde) and

[features. (nanoserde is temporarily unavailable!)](https://github.com/not-fl3/nanoserde)

# bit_vec - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bit-vec/^0.9.1/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#description)Description

Dynamic collections implemented with compact bit vectors.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

This is a simple example of the [Sieve of Eratosthenes](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sieve_of_Eratosthenes)
which calculates prime numbers up to a given limit.

```
use bit_vec::BitVec;
let max_prime = 10000;
// Store the primes as a BitVec
let primes = {
    // Assume all numbers are prime to begin, and then we
    // cross off non-primes progressively
    let mut bv = BitVec::from_elem(max_prime, true);
    // Neither 0 nor 1 are prime
    bv.set(0, false);
    bv.set(1, false);
    for i in 2.. 1 + (max_prime as f64).sqrt() as usize {
        // if i is a prime
        if bv[i] {
            // Mark all multiples of i as non-prime (any multiples below i * i
            // will have been marked as non-prime previously)
            for j in i.. {
                if i * j >= max_prime {
                    break;
                }
                bv.set(i * j, false)
            }
        }
    }
    bv
};
// Simple primality tests below our max bound
let print_primes = 20;
print!("The primes below {} are: ", print_primes);
for x in 0..print_primes {
    if primes.get(x).unwrap_or(false) {
        print!("{} ", x);
    }
}
println!();
let num_primes = primes.iter().filter(|x| *x).count();
println!("There are {} primes below {}", num_primes, max_prime);
assert_eq!(num_primes, 1_229);
```

# borsh - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/borsh/^1.6.0/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#crate-features)Crate features

[§](https://docs.rs#ecosystem-features)Ecosystem features

-
**std**- When enabled,`borsh`uses the standard library. Disabling this feature will result in building the crate in`no_std`environment.To carter such builds, Borsh offers `io``BorshSerialize``BorshDeserialize``io::Read`,`io::Write`and`io::Result`.When **std**feature is enabled, those items are re-exports of corresponding`std::io`items. Otherwise they are borsh-specific types which mimic behaviour of corresponding standard types.

[§](https://docs.rs#default-features)Default features

- **std**- enabled by default.

[§](https://docs.rs#other-features)Other features

-
**derive**- Gates derive macros of[BorshSerialize](https://docs.rs/ser/trait.BorshSerialize.html)and[BorshDeserialize](https://docs.rs/de/trait.BorshDeserialize.html)traits.
-
**unstable__schema**- Gates[BorshSchema](https://docs.rs/schema/trait.BorshSchema.html)trait and its derive macro. Gates[schema](https://docs.rs/schema/index.html)module. This feature requires**derive**to be enabled too.
-
**rc**- Gates implementation of[BorshSerialize](https://docs.rs/ser/trait.BorshSerialize.html)and[BorshDeserialize](https://docs.rs/de/trait.BorshDeserialize.html)for`Rc<T>``Arc<T>``no_std`setting`Rc`/`Arc`are pulled from`alloc`crate. Serializing and deserializing these types does not preserve identity and may result in multiple copies of the same data. Be sure that this is what you want before enabling this feature.
-
**hashbrown**- Pulls in[HashMap](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/collections/hash/map/struct.HashMap.html)/[HashSet](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/collections/hash/set/struct.HashSet.html)when no`std`is available. This feature is set to be mutually exclusive with**std**feature.
-
**bytes**- Gates implementation of[BorshSerialize](https://docs.rs/ser/trait.BorshSerialize.html)and[BorshDeserialize](https://docs.rs/de/trait.BorshDeserialize.html)for[Bytes](https://docs.rs/bytes/1.5.0/bytes/struct.Bytes.html)and[BytesMut](https://docs.rs/bytes/1.5.0/bytes/struct.BytesMut.html). In`no_std`builds this keeps`bytes`in`no_std`mode; when**std**is enabled,`bytes/std`is enabled as well.
-
**bson**- Gates implementation of[BorshSerialize](https://docs.rs/ser/trait.BorshSerialize.html)and[BorshDeserialize](https://docs.rs/de/trait.BorshDeserialize.html)for[ObjectId](https://docs.rs/bson/2.9.0/bson/oid/struct.ObjectId.html).
-
**indexmap**- Gates implementation of[BorshSerialize](https://docs.rs/ser/trait.BorshSerialize.html)and[BorshDeserialize](https://docs.rs/de/trait.BorshDeserialize.html)for[indexmap::IndexMap](https://docs.rs/indexmap/2.8.0/indexmap/map/struct.IndexMap.html)and[IndexSet](https://docs.rs/indexmap/2.8.0/indexmap/set/struct.IndexSet.html)
-
**ascii**- Gates implementation of[BorshSerialize](https://docs.rs/ser/trait.BorshSerialize.html),[BorshDeserialize](https://docs.rs/de/trait.BorshDeserialize.html),[BorshSchema](https://docs.rs/schema/trait.BorshSchema.html)for types from[ascii](https://docs.rs/ascii/1.1.0/ascii/)crate.
-
**de_strict_order**- Enables check that keys, parsed during deserialization of[HashMap](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/collections/hash/map/struct.HashMap.html)/[HashSet](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/collections/hash/set/struct.HashSet.html)and[BTreeSet](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/collections/btree/set/struct.BTreeSet.html)/[BTreeMap](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/collections/btree/map/struct.BTreeMap.html)are encountered in ascending order with respect to[PartialOrd](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/trait.PartialOrd.html)for hash collections, and[Ord](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/trait.Ord.html)for btree ones. Deserialization emits error otherwise.If this feature is not enabled, it is possible that two different byte slices could deserialize into the same `HashMap`/`HashSet`object.

[§](https://docs.rs#config-aliases)Config aliases

- **hash_collections**- This is a feature alias, set up in- `build.rs`to be equivalent to (- **std**OR- **hashbrown**). Gates implementation of- [BorshSerialize](https://docs.rs/ser/trait.BorshSerialize.html),- [BorshDeserialize](https://docs.rs/de/trait.BorshDeserialize.html)and- [BorshSchema](https://docs.rs/schema/trait.BorshSchema.html)for- [HashMap](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/collections/hash/map/struct.HashMap.html)/- [HashSet](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/collections/hash/set/struct.HashSet.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#shortcuts)Shortcuts

Following pages are highlighted here just to give reader a chance at learning that they exist.

# serde - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde/^1.0/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#serde)Serde

Serde is a framework for * ser*ializing and

*serializing Rust data structures efficiently and generically.*

**de**The Serde ecosystem consists of data structures that know how to serialize and deserialize themselves along with data formats that know how to serialize and deserialize other things. Serde provides the layer by which these two groups interact with each other, allowing any supported data structure to be serialized and deserialized using any supported data format.

See the Serde website [https://serde.rs](https://serde.rs) for additional documentation and
usage examples.

[§](https://docs.rs#design)Design

Where many other languages rely on runtime reflection for serializing data,
Serde is instead built on Rust’s powerful trait system. A data structure
that knows how to serialize and deserialize itself is one that implements
Serde’s `Serialize` and `Deserialize` traits (or uses Serde’s derive
attribute to automatically generate implementations at compile time). This
avoids any overhead of reflection or runtime type information. In fact in
many situations the interaction between data structure and data format can
be completely optimized away by the Rust compiler, leaving Serde
serialization to perform the same speed as a handwritten serializer for the
specific selection of data structure and data format.

[§](https://docs.rs#data-formats)Data formats

The following is a partial list of data formats that have been implemented for Serde by the community.

- [JSON](https://github.com/serde-rs/json), the ubiquitous JavaScript Object Notation used by many HTTP APIs.
- [Postcard](https://github.com/jamesmunns/postcard), a no_std and embedded-systems friendly compact binary format.
- [CBOR](https://github.com/enarx/ciborium), a Concise Binary Object Representation designed for small message size without the need for version negotiation.
- [YAML](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-yaml), a self-proclaimed human-friendly configuration language that ain’t markup language.
- [MessagePack](https://github.com/3Hren/msgpack-rust), an efficient binary format that resembles a compact JSON.
- [TOML](https://docs.rs/toml), a minimal configuration format used by- [Cargo](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html).
- [Pickle](https://github.com/birkenfeld/serde-pickle), a format common in the Python world.
- [RON](https://github.com/ron-rs/ron), a Rusty Object Notation.
- [BSON](https://github.com/mongodb/bson-rust), the data storage and network transfer format used by MongoDB.
- [Avro](https://docs.rs/apache-avro), a binary format used within Apache Hadoop, with support for schema definition.
- [JSON5](https://github.com/callum-oakley/json5-rs), a superset of JSON including some productions from ES5.
- [URL](https://docs.rs/serde_qs)query strings, in the x-www-form-urlencoded format.
- [Starlark](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-starlark), the format used for describing build targets by the Bazel and Buck build systems.- *(serialization only)*
- [Envy](https://github.com/softprops/envy), a way to deserialize environment variables into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [Envy Store](https://github.com/softprops/envy-store), a way to deserialize- [AWS Parameter Store](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/systems-manager-parameter-store.html)parameters into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [S-expressions](https://github.com/rotty/lexpr-rs), the textual representation of code and data used by the Lisp language family.
- [D-Bus](https://docs.rs/zvariant)’s binary wire format.
- [FlexBuffers](https://github.com/google/flatbuffers/tree/master/rust/flexbuffers), the schemaless cousin of Google’s FlatBuffers zero-copy serialization format.
- [Bencode](https://github.com/P3KI/bendy), a simple binary format used in the BitTorrent protocol.
- [Token streams](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/serde_tokenstream), for processing Rust procedural macro input.- *(deserialization only)*
- [DynamoDB Items](https://docs.rs/serde_dynamo), the format used by- [rusoto_dynamodb](https://docs.rs/rusoto_dynamodb)to transfer data to and from DynamoDB.
- [Hjson](https://github.com/Canop/deser-hjson), a syntax extension to JSON designed around human reading and editing.- *(deserialization only)*
- [CSV](https://docs.rs/csv), Comma-separated values is a tabular text file format.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be deserialized from any data format supported by Serde.
- [Deserializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserializer.html)
- A **data format**that can deserialize any data structure supported by Serde.
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Serialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be serialized into any data format supported by Serde.
- [Serializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html)
- A **data format**that can serialize any data structure supported by Serde.

- Derive macro available if serde is built with `features = ["derive"]`.

# rand - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand/^0.9/

## Expand description

Utilities for random number generation

Rand provides utilities to generate random numbers, to convert them to useful types and distributions, and some randomness-related algorithms.

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

```
// The prelude import enables methods we use below, specifically
// Rng::random, Rng::sample, SliceRandom::shuffle and IndexedRandom::choose.
use rand::prelude::*;
// Get an RNG:
let mut rng = rand::rng();
// Try printing a random unicode code point (probably a bad idea)!
println!("char: '{}'", rng.random::<char>());
// Try printing a random alphanumeric value instead!
println!("alpha: '{}'", rng.sample(rand::distr::Alphanumeric) as char);
// Generate and shuffle a sequence:
let mut nums: Vec<i32> = (1..100).collect();
nums.shuffle(&mut rng);
// And take a random pick (yes, we didn't need to shuffle first!):
let _ = nums.choose(&mut rng);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#the-book)The Book

For the user guide and further documentation, please read
[The Rust Rand Book](https://rust-random.github.io/book).

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use`- [rand_core](https://docs.rs/rand_core/0.9.5/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand_core/index.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

# serde_json - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde_json/^1.0/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#serde-json)Serde JSON

JSON is a ubiquitous open-standard format that uses human-readable text to transmit data objects consisting of key-value pairs.

```
{
    "name": "John Doe",
    "age": 43,
    "address": {
        "street": "10 Downing Street",
        "city": "London"
    },
    "phones": [
        "+44 1234567",
        "+44 2345678"
    ]
}
```
There are three common ways that you might find yourself needing to work with JSON data in Rust.

- **As text data.**An unprocessed string of JSON data that you receive on an HTTP endpoint, read from a file, or prepare to send to a remote server.
- **As an untyped or loosely typed representation.**Maybe you want to check that some JSON data is valid before passing it on, but without knowing the structure of what it contains. Or you want to do very basic manipulations like insert a key in a particular spot.
- **As a strongly typed Rust data structure.**When you expect all or most of your data to conform to a particular structure and want to get real work done without JSON’s loosey-goosey nature tripping you up.

Serde JSON provides efficient, flexible, safe ways of converting data between each of these representations.

[§](https://docs.rs#operating-on-untyped-json-values)Operating on untyped JSON values

Any valid JSON data can be manipulated in the following recursive enum
representation. This data structure is [ serde_json::Value](https://docs.rs/enum.Value.html).

```
enum Value {
    Null,
    Bool(bool),
    Number(Number),
    String(String),
    Array(Vec<Value>),
    Object(Map<String, Value>),
}
```
A string of JSON data can be parsed into a `serde_json::Value` by the
[ serde_json::from_str](https://docs.rs/fn.from_str.html) function. There is also

[for parsing from a byte slice](https://docs.rs/fn.from_slice.html)

`from_slice``&[u8]` and [for parsing from any](https://docs.rs/fn.from_reader.html)

`from_reader``io::Read` like a File or a TCP stream.```
use serde_json::{Result, Value};
fn untyped_example() -> Result<()> {
    // Some JSON input data as a &str. Maybe this comes from the user.
    let data = r#"
        {
            "name": "John Doe",
            "age": 43,
            "phones": [
                "+44 1234567",
                "+44 2345678"
            ]
        }"#;
    // Parse the string of data into serde_json::Value.
    let v: Value = serde_json::from_str(data)?;
    // Access parts of the data by indexing with square brackets.
    println!("Please call {} at the number {}", v["name"], v["phones"][0]);
    Ok(())
}
```
The result of square bracket indexing like `v["name"]` is a borrow of the
data at that index, so the type is `&Value`. A JSON map can be indexed with
string keys, while a JSON array can be indexed with integer keys. If the
type of the data is not right for the type with which it is being indexed,
or if a map does not contain the key being indexed, or if the index into a
vector is out of bounds, the returned element is `Value::Null`.

When a `Value` is printed, it is printed as a JSON string. So in the code
above, the output looks like `Please call "John Doe" at the number "+44 1234567"`. The quotation marks appear because `v["name"]` is a `&Value`
containing a JSON string and its JSON representation is `"John Doe"`.
Printing as a plain string without quotation marks involves converting from
a JSON string to a Rust string with [ as_str()](https://docs.rs/enum.Value.html#method.as_str) or avoiding the use of

`Value` as described in the following section.The `Value` representation is sufficient for very basic tasks but can be
tedious to work with for anything more significant. Error handling is
verbose to implement correctly, for example imagine trying to detect the
presence of unrecognized fields in the input data. The compiler is powerless
to help you when you make a mistake, for example imagine typoing `v["name"]`
as `v["nmae"]` in one of the dozens of places it is used in your code.

[§](https://docs.rs#parsing-json-as-strongly-typed-data-structures)Parsing JSON as strongly typed data structures

Serde provides a powerful way of mapping JSON data into Rust data structures largely automatically.

```
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
use serde_json::Result;
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
struct Person {
    name: String,
    age: u8,
    phones: Vec<String>,
}
fn typed_example() -> Result<()> {
    // Some JSON input data as a &str. Maybe this comes from the user.
    let data = r#"
        {
            "name": "John Doe",
            "age": 43,
            "phones": [
                "+44 1234567",
                "+44 2345678"
            ]
        }"#;
    // Parse the string of data into a Person object. This is exactly the
    // same function as the one that produced serde_json::Value above, but
    // now we are asking it for a Person as output.
    let p: Person = serde_json::from_str(data)?;
    // Do things just like with any other Rust data structure.
    println!("Please call {} at the number {}", p.name, p.phones[0]);
    Ok(())
}
```
This is the same `serde_json::from_str` function as before, but this time we
assign the return value to a variable of type `Person` so Serde will
automatically interpret the input data as a `Person` and produce informative
error messages if the layout does not conform to what a `Person` is expected
to look like.

Any type that implements Serde’s `Deserialize` trait can be deserialized
this way. This includes built-in Rust standard library types like `Vec<T>`
and `HashMap<K, V>`, as well as any structs or enums annotated with
`#[derive(Deserialize)]`.

Once we have `p` of type `Person`, our IDE and the Rust compiler can help us
use it correctly like they do for any other Rust code. The IDE can
autocomplete field names to prevent typos, which was impossible in the
`serde_json::Value` representation. And the Rust compiler can check that
when we write `p.phones[0]`, then `p.phones` is guaranteed to be a
`Vec<String>` so indexing into it makes sense and produces a `String`.

[§](https://docs.rs#constructing-json-values)Constructing JSON values

Serde JSON provides a [ json! macro](https://docs.rs/macro.json.html) to build

`serde_json::Value`
objects with very natural JSON syntax.```
use serde_json::json;
fn main() {
    // The type of `john` is `serde_json::Value`
    let john = json!({
        "name": "John Doe",
        "age": 43,
        "phones": [
            "+44 1234567",
            "+44 2345678"
        ]
    });
    println!("first phone number: {}", john["phones"][0]);
    // Convert to a string of JSON and print it out
    println!("{}", john.to_string());
}
```
The `Value::to_string()` function converts a `serde_json::Value` into a
`String` of JSON text.

One neat thing about the `json!` macro is that variables and expressions can
be interpolated directly into the JSON value as you are building it. Serde
will check at compile time that the value you are interpolating is able to
be represented as JSON.

```
let full_name = "John Doe";
let age_last_year = 42;
// The type of `john` is `serde_json::Value`
let john = json!({
    "name": full_name,
    "age": age_last_year + 1,
    "phones": [
        format!("+44 {}", random_phone())
    ]
});
```
This is amazingly convenient, but we have the problem we had before with
`Value`: the IDE and Rust compiler cannot help us if we get it wrong. Serde
JSON provides a better way of serializing strongly-typed data structures
into JSON text.

[§](https://docs.rs#creating-json-by-serializing-data-structures)Creating JSON by serializing data structures

A data structure can be converted to a JSON string by
[ serde_json::to_string](https://docs.rs/fn.to_string.html). There is also

[which serializes to a](https://docs.rs/fn.to_vec.html)

`serde_json::to_vec``Vec<u8>` and
[which serializes to any](https://docs.rs/fn.to_writer.html)

`serde_json::to_writer``io::Write`
such as a File or a TCP stream.```
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
use serde_json::Result;
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
struct Address {
    street: String,
    city: String,
}
fn print_an_address() -> Result<()> {
    // Some data structure.
    let address = Address {
        street: "10 Downing Street".to_owned(),
        city: "London".to_owned(),
    };
    // Serialize it to a JSON string.
    let j = serde_json::to_string(&address)?;
    // Print, write to a file, or send to an HTTP server.
    println!("{}", j);
    Ok(())
}
```
Any type that implements Serde’s `Serialize` trait can be serialized this
way. This includes built-in Rust standard library types like `Vec<T>` and
`HashMap<K, V>`, as well as any structs or enums annotated with
`#[derive(Serialize)]`.

[§](https://docs.rs#no-std-support)No-std support

As long as there is a memory allocator, it is possible to use serde_json without the rest of the Rust standard library. Disable the default “std” feature and enable the “alloc” feature:

```
[dependencies]
serde_json = { version = "1.0", default-features = false, features = ["alloc"] }
```
For JSON support in Serde without a memory allocator, please see the
[ serde-json-core](https://github.com/rust-embedded-community/serde-json-core) crate.

# bit_set - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/bit-set/latest/target-redirect/aarch64-apple-darwin/bit_set/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#description)Description

An implementation of a set using a bit vector as an underlying representation for holding unsigned numerical elements.

It should also be noted that the amount of storage necessary for holding a
set of objects is proportional to the maximum of the objects when viewed
as a `usize`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use bit_set::BitSet;
// It's a regular set
let mut s = BitSet::new();
s.insert(0);
s.insert(3);
s.insert(7);
s.remove(7);
if !s.contains(7) {
    println!("There is no 7");
}
// Can initialize from a `BitVec`
let other = BitSet::from_bytes(&[0b11010000]);
s.union_with(&other);
// Print 0, 1, 3 in some order
for x in s.iter() {
    println!("{}", x);
}
// Can convert back to a `BitVec`
let bv = s.into_bit_vec();
assert!(bv[3]);
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [BitSet](https://docs.rs/struct.BitSet.html)
- [Difference](https://docs.rs/struct.Difference.html)
- [Intersection](https://docs.rs/struct.Intersection.html)
- [Iter](https://docs.rs/struct.Iter.html)
- An iterator for `BitSet`.
- [Symmetric](https://docs.rs/struct.SymmetricDifference.html)- Difference
- [Union](https://docs.rs/struct.Union.html)

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [BitBlock](https://docs.rs/trait.BitBlock.html)
- Abstracts over a pile of bits (basically unsigned primitives)

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (4c9d2bfe4 2026-07-01)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

## Usage

Add this to your Cargo.toml:

```
[]
 = "0.10"
```
Since Rust 2018, `extern crate` is no longer mandatory. If your edition is old (Rust 2015),
add this to your crate root:

```
extern crate bit_set;
```
If you want to use `serde`, enable it with the `serde` feature:

```
[]
 = {  = "0.10",  = ["serde"] }
```
If you want to use bit-set in a program that has `#![no_std]`, just drop default features:

```
[]
 = {  = "0.10",  = false }
```
If you want to use serde with the alloc crate instead of std, just use the `serde_no_std` feature:

```
[]
 = {  = "0.10",  = false,  = ["serde", "serde_no_std"] }
```
If you want [borsh-rs](https://github.com/near/borsh-rs) support, include it like this:

```
[]
 = {  = "0.10",  = ["borsh"] }
```
Other available serialization libraries can be enabled with the
[ miniserde](https://github.com/dtolnay/miniserde) and

[features. (nanoserde is temporarily unavailable!)](https://github.com/not-fl3/nanoserde)

# bit_set - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/bit-set/0.10.0/target-redirect/aarch64-apple-darwin/bit_set/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#description)Description

An implementation of a set using a bit vector as an underlying representation for holding unsigned numerical elements.

It should also be noted that the amount of storage necessary for holding a
set of objects is proportional to the maximum of the objects when viewed
as a `usize`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use bit_set::BitSet;
// It's a regular set
let mut s = BitSet::new();
s.insert(0);
s.insert(3);
s.insert(7);
s.remove(7);
if !s.contains(7) {
    println!("There is no 7");
}
// Can initialize from a `BitVec`
let other = BitSet::from_bytes(&[0b11010000]);
s.union_with(&other);
// Print 0, 1, 3 in some order
for x in s.iter() {
    println!("{}", x);
}
// Can convert back to a `BitVec`
let bv = s.into_bit_vec();
assert!(bv[3]);
```

- [BitSet](https://docs.rs/struct.BitSet.html)
- [Difference](https://docs.rs/struct.Difference.html)
- [Intersection](https://docs.rs/struct.Intersection.html)
- [Iter](https://docs.rs/struct.Iter.html)
- An iterator for `BitSet`.
- [Symmetric](https://docs.rs/struct.SymmetricDifference.html)- Difference
- [Union](https://docs.rs/struct.Union.html)

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [BitBlock](https://docs.rs/trait.BitBlock.html)
- Abstracts over a pile of bits (basically unsigned primitives)

[78](https://docs.rs#78)/// Computes how many blocks are needed to store that many bits
[79](https://docs.rs#79)fn blocks_for_bits<B: BitBlock>(bits: usize) -> usize {
[80](https://docs.rs#80)    // If we want 17 bits, dividing by 32 will produce 0. So we add 1 to make sure we
[81](https://docs.rs#81)    // reserve enough. But if we want exactly a multiple of 32, this will actually allocate
[82](https://docs.rs#82)    // one too many. So we need to check if that's the case. We can do that by computing if
[83](https://docs.rs#83)    // bitwise AND by `32 - 1` is 0. But LLVM should be able to optimize the semantically
[84](https://docs.rs#84)    // superior modulo operator on a power of two to this.
[85](https://docs.rs#85)    //
[86](https://docs.rs#86)    // Note that we can technically avoid this branch with the expression
[87](https://docs.rs#87)    // `(nbits + BITS - 1) / 32::BITS`, but if nbits is almost usize::MAX this will overflow.
[88](https://docs.rs#88)    if bits % B::bits() == 0 {
[89](https://docs.rs#89)        bits / B::bits()
[90](https://docs.rs#90)    } else {
[91](https://docs.rs#91)        bits / B::bits() + 1
[92](https://docs.rs#92)    }
[93](https://docs.rs#93)}
[94](https://docs.rs#94)
[95](https://docs.rs#95)#[allow(clippy::iter_skip_zero)]
[96](https://docs.rs#96)// Take two BitVec's, and return iterators of their words, where the shorter one
[97](https://docs.rs#97)// has been padded with 0's
[98](https://docs.rs#98)fn match_words<'a, 'b, B: BitBlock>(
[99](https://docs.rs#99)    a: &'a BitVec<B>,
[100](https://docs.rs#100)    b: &'b BitVec<B>,
[101](https://docs.rs#101)) -> (MatchWords<'a, B>, MatchWords<'b, B>) {
[102](https://docs.rs#102)    let a_len = a.storage().len();
[103](https://docs.rs#103)    let b_len = b.storage().len();
[104](https://docs.rs#104)
[105](https://docs.rs#105)    // have to uselessly pretend to pad the longer one for type matching
[106](https://docs.rs#106)    if a_len < b_len {
[107](https://docs.rs#107)        (
[108](https://docs.rs#108)            a.blocks()
[109](https://docs.rs#109)                .enumerate()
[110](https://docs.rs#110)                .chain(iter::repeat(B::zero()).enumerate().take(b_len).skip(a_len)),
[111](https://docs.rs#111)            b.blocks()
[112](https://docs.rs#112)                .enumerate()
[113](https://docs.rs#113)                .chain(iter::repeat(B::zero()).enumerate().take(0).skip(0)),
[114](https://docs.rs#114)        )
[115](https://docs.rs#115)    } else {
[116](https://docs.rs#116)        (
[117](https://docs.rs#117)            a.blocks()
[118](https://docs.rs#118)                .enumerate()
[119](https://docs.rs#119)                .chain(iter::repeat(B::zero()).enumerate().take(0).skip(0)),
[120](https://docs.rs#120)            b.blocks()
[121](https://docs.rs#121)                .enumerate()
[122](https://docs.rs#122)                .chain(iter::repeat(B::zero()).enumerate().take(a_len).skip(b_len)),
[123](https://docs.rs#123)        )
[124](https://docs.rs#124)    }
[125](https://docs.rs#125)}

[340](https://docs.rs#340)    /// Reserves capacity for the given `BitSet` to contain `len` distinct elements. In the case
[341](https://docs.rs#341)    /// of `BitSet` this means reallocations will not occur as long as all inserted elements
[342](https://docs.rs#342)    /// are less than `len`.
[343](https://docs.rs#343)    ///
[344](https://docs.rs#344)    /// The collection may reserve more space to avoid frequent reallocations.
[345](https://docs.rs#345)    ///
[346](https://docs.rs#346)    ///
[347](https://docs.rs#347)    /// # Examples
[348](https://docs.rs#348)    ///
[349](https://docs.rs#349)    /// ```
[350](https://docs.rs#350)    /// use bit_set::BitSet;
[351](https://docs.rs#351)    ///
[352](https://docs.rs#352)    /// let mut s = BitSet::new();
[353](https://docs.rs#353)    /// s.reserve_len(10);
[354](https://docs.rs#354)    /// assert!(s.capacity() >= 10);
[355](https://docs.rs#355)    /// ```
[356](https://docs.rs#356)    pub fn reserve_len(&mut self, len: usize) {
[357](https://docs.rs#357)        let cur_len = self.bit_vec.len();
[358](https://docs.rs#358)        if len >= cur_len {
[359](https://docs.rs#359)            self.bit_vec.reserve(len - cur_len);
[360](https://docs.rs#360)        }
[361](https://docs.rs#361)    }
[362](https://docs.rs#362)
[363](https://docs.rs#363)    /// Reserves the minimum capacity for the given `BitSet` to contain `len` distinct elements.
[364](https://docs.rs#364)    /// In the case of `BitSet` this means reallocations will not occur as long as all inserted
[365](https://docs.rs#365)    /// elements are less than `len`.
[366](https://docs.rs#366)    ///
[367](https://docs.rs#367)    /// Note that the allocator may give the collection more space than it requests. Therefore
[368](https://docs.rs#368)    /// capacity can not be relied upon to be precisely minimal. Prefer `reserve_len` if future
[369](https://docs.rs#369)    /// insertions are expected.
[370](https://docs.rs#370)    ///
[371](https://docs.rs#371)    ///
[372](https://docs.rs#372)    /// # Examples
[373](https://docs.rs#373)    ///
[374](https://docs.rs#374)    /// ```
[375](https://docs.rs#375)    /// use bit_set::BitSet;
[376](https://docs.rs#376)    ///
[377](https://docs.rs#377)    /// let mut s = BitSet::new();
[378](https://docs.rs#378)    /// s.reserve_len_exact(10);
[379](https://docs.rs#379)    /// assert!(s.capacity() >= 10);
[380](https://docs.rs#380)    /// ```
[381](https://docs.rs#381)    pub fn reserve_len_exact(&mut self, len: usize) {
[382](https://docs.rs#382)        let cur_len = self.bit_vec.len();
[383](https://docs.rs#383)        if len >= cur_len {
[384](https://docs.rs#384)            self.bit_vec.reserve_exact(len - cur_len);
[385](https://docs.rs#385)        }
[386](https://docs.rs#386)    }

[451](https://docs.rs#451)    #[inline]
[452](https://docs.rs#452)    fn other_op<F>(&mut self, other: &Self, mut f: F)
[453](https://docs.rs#453)    where
[454](https://docs.rs#454)        F: FnMut(B, B) -> B,
[455](https://docs.rs#455)    {
[456](https://docs.rs#456)        // Unwrap BitVecs
[457](https://docs.rs#457)        let self_bit_vec = &mut self.bit_vec;
[458](https://docs.rs#458)        let other_bit_vec = &other.bit_vec;
[459](https://docs.rs#459)
[460](https://docs.rs#460)        let self_len = self_bit_vec.len();
[461](https://docs.rs#461)        let other_len = other_bit_vec.len();
[462](https://docs.rs#462)
[463](https://docs.rs#463)        // Expand the vector if necessary
[464](https://docs.rs#464)        if self_len < other_len {
[465](https://docs.rs#465)            self_bit_vec.grow(other_len - self_len, false);
[466](https://docs.rs#466)        }
[467](https://docs.rs#467)
[468](https://docs.rs#468)        // virtually pad other with 0's for equal lengths
[469](https://docs.rs#469)        let other_words = {
[470](https://docs.rs#470)            let (_, result) = match_words(self_bit_vec, other_bit_vec);
[471](https://docs.rs#471)            result
[472](https://docs.rs#472)        };
[473](https://docs.rs#473)
[474](https://docs.rs#474)        // Apply values found in other
[475](https://docs.rs#475)        for (i, w) in other_words {
[476](https://docs.rs#476)            let old = self_bit_vec.storage()[i];
[477](https://docs.rs#477)            let new = f(old, w);
[478](https://docs.rs#478)            unsafe {
[479](https://docs.rs#479)                self_bit_vec.storage_mut()[i] = new;
[480](https://docs.rs#480)            }
[481](https://docs.rs#481)        }
[482](https://docs.rs#482)    }
[483](https://docs.rs#483)
[484](https://docs.rs#484)    /// Truncates the underlying vector to the least length required.
[485](https://docs.rs#485)    ///
[486](https://docs.rs#486)    /// # Examples
[487](https://docs.rs#487)    ///
[488](https://docs.rs#488)    /// ```
[489](https://docs.rs#489)    /// use bit_set::BitSet;
[490](https://docs.rs#490)    ///
[491](https://docs.rs#491)    /// let mut s = BitSet::new();
[492](https://docs.rs#492)    /// s.insert(3231);
[493](https://docs.rs#493)    /// s.remove(3231);
[494](https://docs.rs#494)    ///
[495](https://docs.rs#495)    /// // Internal storage will probably be bigger than necessary
[496](https://docs.rs#496)    /// println!("old capacity: {}", s.capacity());
[497](https://docs.rs#497)    /// assert!(s.capacity() >= 3231);
[498](https://docs.rs#498)    ///
[499](https://docs.rs#499)    /// // Now should be smaller
[500](https://docs.rs#500)    /// s.shrink_to_fit();
[501](https://docs.rs#501)    /// println!("new capacity: {}", s.capacity());
[502](https://docs.rs#502)    /// ```
[503](https://docs.rs#503)    #[inline]
[504](https://docs.rs#504)    pub fn shrink_to_fit(&mut self) {
[505](https://docs.rs#505)        let bit_vec = &mut self.bit_vec;
[506](https://docs.rs#506)        // Obtain original length
[507](https://docs.rs#507)        let old_len = bit_vec.storage().len();
[508](https://docs.rs#508)        // Obtain coarse trailing zero length
[509](https://docs.rs#509)        let n = bit_vec
[510](https://docs.rs#510)            .storage()
[511](https://docs.rs#511)            .iter()
[512](https://docs.rs#512)            .rev()
[513](https://docs.rs#513)            .take_while(|&&n| n == B::zero())
[514](https://docs.rs#514)            .count();
[515](https://docs.rs#515)        // Truncate away all empty trailing blocks, then shrink_to_fit
[516](https://docs.rs#516)        let trunc_len = old_len - n;
[517](https://docs.rs#517)        unsafe {
[518](https://docs.rs#518)            bit_vec.storage_mut().truncate(trunc_len);
[519](https://docs.rs#519)            bit_vec.set_len(trunc_len * B::bits());
[520](https://docs.rs#520)        }
[521](https://docs.rs#521)        bit_vec.shrink_to_fit();
[522](https://docs.rs#522)    }

[828](https://docs.rs#828)        /// ```
[829](https://docs.rs#829)        pub fn split_off(&mut self, at: usize) -> Self {
[830](https://docs.rs#830)            let mut other = BitSet::new();
[831](https://docs.rs#831)
[832](https://docs.rs#832)            if at == 0 {
[833](https://docs.rs#833)                swap(self, &mut other);
[834](https://docs.rs#834)                return other;
[835](https://docs.rs#835)            } else if at >= self.bit_vec.len() {
[836](https://docs.rs#836)                return other;
[837](https://docs.rs#837)            }
[838](https://docs.rs#838)
[839](https://docs.rs#839)            // Calculate block and bit at which to split
[840](https://docs.rs#840)            let w = at / BITS;
[841](https://docs.rs#841)            let b = at % BITS;
[842](https://docs.rs#842)
[843](https://docs.rs#843)            // Pad `other` with `w` zero blocks,
[844](https://docs.rs#844)            // append `self`'s blocks in the range from `w` to the end to `other`
[845](https://docs.rs#845)            other.bit_vec.storage_mut().extend(repeat(0u32).take(w)
[846](https://docs.rs#846)                                         .chain(self.bit_vec.storage()[w..].iter().cloned()));
[847](https://docs.rs#847)            other.bit_vec.nbits = self.bit_vec.nbits;
[848](https://docs.rs#848)
[849](https://docs.rs#849)            if b > 0 {
[850](https://docs.rs#850)                other.bit_vec.storage_mut()[w] &= !0 << b;
[851](https://docs.rs#851)            }
[852](https://docs.rs#852)
[853](https://docs.rs#853)            // Sets `bit_vec.len()` and fixes the last block as well
[854](https://docs.rs#854)            self.bit_vec.truncate(at);
[855](https://docs.rs#855)
[856](https://docs.rs#856)            other
[857](https://docs.rs#857)        }
[858](https://docs.rs#858)    */
[859](https://docs.rs#859)

[928](https://docs.rs#928)        let other_bit_vec = &other.bit_vec;
[929](https://docs.rs#929)        let other_blocks = blocks_for_bits::<B>(other_bit_vec.len());
[930](https://docs.rs#930)
[931](https://docs.rs#931)        // Check that `self` intersect `other` is self
[932](https://docs.rs#932)        self_bit_vec.blocks().zip(other_bit_vec.blocks()).all(|(w1, w2)| w1 & w2 == w1) &&
[933](https://docs.rs#933)        // Make sure if `self` has any more blocks than `other`, they're all 0
[934](https://docs.rs#934)        self_bit_vec.blocks().skip(other_blocks).all(|w| w == B::zero())

[943](https://docs.rs#943)    /// Adds a value to the set. Returns `true` if the value was not already

[945](https://docs.rs#945)    pub fn insert(&mut self, value: usize) -> bool {
[946](https://docs.rs#946)        if self.contains(value) {
[947](https://docs.rs#947)            return false;
[948](https://docs.rs#948)        }
[949](https://docs.rs#949)
[950](https://docs.rs#950)        // Ensure we have enough space to hold the new element

[954](https://docs.rs#954)        }

[957](https://docs.rs#957)        true
[958](https://docs.rs#958)    }

[968](https://docs.rs#968)
[969](https://docs.rs#969)        true
[970](https://docs.rs#970)    }

[1048](https://docs.rs#1048)impl<T, B: BitBlock> Iterator for BlockIter<T, B>
[1049](https://docs.rs#1049)where
[1050](https://docs.rs#1050)    T: Iterator<Item = B>,
[1051](https://docs.rs#1051){
[1052](https://docs.rs#1052)    type Item = usize;
[1053](https://docs.rs#1053)
[1054](https://docs.rs#1054)    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<usize> {
[1055](https://docs.rs#1055)        while self.head == B::zero() {
[1056](https://docs.rs#1056)            match self.tail.next() {
[1057](https://docs.rs#1057)                Some(w) => self.head = w,
[1058](https://docs.rs#1058)                None => return None,
[1059](https://docs.rs#1059)            }
[1060](https://docs.rs#1060)            self.head_offset += B::bits();
[1061](https://docs.rs#1061)        }
[1062](https://docs.rs#1062)
[1063](https://docs.rs#1063)        // from the current block, isolate the
[1064](https://docs.rs#1064)        // LSB and subtract 1, producing k:
[1065](https://docs.rs#1065)        // a block with a number of set bits
[1066](https://docs.rs#1066)        // equal to the index of the LSB
[1067](https://docs.rs#1067)        let k = (self.head & (!self.head + B::one())) - B::one();
[1068](https://docs.rs#1068)        // update block, removing the LSB
[1069](https://docs.rs#1069)        self.head = self.head & (self.head - B::one());
[1070](https://docs.rs#1070)        // return offset + (index of LSB)
[1071](https://docs.rs#1071)        Some(self.head_offset + (B::count_ones(k)))
[1072](https://docs.rs#1072)    }
[1073](https://docs.rs#1073)
[1074](https://docs.rs#1074)    fn count(self) -> usize {
[1075](https://docs.rs#1075)        self.head.count_ones() + self.tail.map(|block| block.count_ones()).sum::<usize>()
[1076](https://docs.rs#1076)    }
[1077](https://docs.rs#1077)
[1078](https://docs.rs#1078)    #[inline]
[1079](https://docs.rs#1079)    fn size_hint(&self) -> (usize, Option<usize>) {
[1080](https://docs.rs#1080)        match self.tail.size_hint() {
[1081](https://docs.rs#1081)            (_, Some(h)) => (0, Some((1 + h) * B::bits())),
[1082](https://docs.rs#1082)            _ => (0, None),
[1083](https://docs.rs#1083)        }
[1084](https://docs.rs#1084)    }

[1100](https://docs.rs#1100)    fn size_hint(&self) -> (usize, Option<usize>) {

[1102](https://docs.rs#1102)        let (second_lower_bound, second_upper_bound) = self.other.size_hint();
[1103](https://docs.rs#1103)

[1105](https://docs.rs#1105)

[1107](https://docs.rs#1107)        (
[1108](https://docs.rs#1108)            cmp::max(first_lower_bound, second_lower_bound),
[1109](https://docs.rs#1109)            upper_bound.map(get_max),

[1111](https://docs.rs#1111)    }

[1417](https://docs.rs#1417)    fn test_bit_set_subset() {
[1418](https://docs.rs#1418)        let mut set1 = BitSet::new();
[1419](https://docs.rs#1419)        let mut set2 = BitSet::new();
[1420](https://docs.rs#1420)
[1421](https://docs.rs#1421)        assert!(set1.is_subset(&set2)); //  {}  {}
[1422](https://docs.rs#1422)        set2.insert(100);
[1423](https://docs.rs#1423)        assert!(set1.is_subset(&set2)); //  {}  { 1 }
[1424](https://docs.rs#1424)        set2.insert(200);
[1425](https://docs.rs#1425)        assert!(set1.is_subset(&set2)); //  {}  { 1, 2 }
[1426](https://docs.rs#1426)        set1.insert(200);
[1427](https://docs.rs#1427)        assert!(set1.is_subset(&set2)); //  { 2 }  { 1, 2 }
[1428](https://docs.rs#1428)        set1.insert(300);
[1429](https://docs.rs#1429)        assert!(!set1.is_subset(&set2)); // { 2, 3 }  { 1, 2 }
[1430](https://docs.rs#1430)        set2.insert(300);
[1431](https://docs.rs#1431)        assert!(set1.is_subset(&set2)); // { 2, 3 }  { 1, 2, 3 }
[1432](https://docs.rs#1432)        set2.insert(400);
[1433](https://docs.rs#1433)        assert!(set1.is_subset(&set2)); // { 2, 3 }  { 1, 2, 3, 4 }
[1434](https://docs.rs#1434)        set2.remove(100);
[1435](https://docs.rs#1435)        assert!(set1.is_subset(&set2)); // { 2, 3 }  { 2, 3, 4 }
[1436](https://docs.rs#1436)        set2.remove(300);
[1437](https://docs.rs#1437)        assert!(!set1.is_subset(&set2)); // { 2, 3 }  { 2, 4 }
[1438](https://docs.rs#1438)        set1.remove(300);
[1439](https://docs.rs#1439)        assert!(set1.is_subset(&set2)); // { 2 }  { 2, 4 }
[1440](https://docs.rs#1440)    }

[1503](https://docs.rs#1503)        let mut b = BitSet::from_bytes(&[0b01100010]);

[1506](https://docs.rs#1506)        b.intersect_with(&c);

[1512](https://docs.rs#1512)    fn test_bit_set_difference_with() {
[1513](https://docs.rs#1513)        // Explicitly 0'ed bits
[1514](https://docs.rs#1514)        let mut a = BitSet::from_bytes(&[0b00000000]);

[1518](https://docs.rs#1518)
[1519](https://docs.rs#1519)        // Uninitialized bits should behave like 0's

[1524](https://docs.rs#1524)

[1593](https://docs.rs#1593)    fn test_bit_set_shrink_to_fit_new() {

[1595](https://docs.rs#1595)        // and this would end up actually growing the array in a way
[1596](https://docs.rs#1596)        // that (safely corrupted the state).
[1597](https://docs.rs#1597)        let mut a = BitSet::new();
[1598](https://docs.rs#1598)        assert_eq!(a.count(), 0);
[1599](https://docs.rs#1599)        assert_eq!(a.capacity(), 0);
[1600](https://docs.rs#1600)        a.shrink_to_fit();
[1601](https://docs.rs#1601)        assert_eq!(a.count(), 0);
[1602](https://docs.rs#1602)        assert_eq!(a.capacity(), 0);
[1603](https://docs.rs#1603)        assert!(!a.contains(1));
[1604](https://docs.rs#1604)        a.insert(3);
[1605](https://docs.rs#1605)        assert!(a.contains(3));
[1606](https://docs.rs#1606)        assert_eq!(a.count(), 1);
[1607](https://docs.rs#1607)        assert!(a.capacity() > 0);
[1608](https://docs.rs#1608)        a.shrink_to_fit();
[1609](https://docs.rs#1609)        assert!(a.contains(3));
[1610](https://docs.rs#1610)        assert_eq!(a.count(), 1);
[1611](https://docs.rs#1611)        assert!(a.capacity() > 0);
[1612](https://docs.rs#1612)    }

[1614](https://docs.rs#1614)    #[test]
[1615](https://docs.rs#1615)    fn test_bit_set_shrink_to_fit() {
[1616](https://docs.rs#1616)        let mut a = BitSet::new();
[1617](https://docs.rs#1617)        assert_eq!(a.count(), 0);
[1618](https://docs.rs#1618)        assert_eq!(a.capacity(), 0);
[1619](https://docs.rs#1619)        a.insert(259);
[1620](https://docs.rs#1620)        a.insert(98);
[1621](https://docs.rs#1621)        a.insert(3);
[1622](https://docs.rs#1622)        assert_eq!(a.count(), 3);
[1623](https://docs.rs#1623)        assert!(a.capacity() > 0);
[1624](https://docs.rs#1624)        assert!(!a.contains(1));
[1625](https://docs.rs#1625)        assert!(a.contains(259));
[1626](https://docs.rs#1626)        assert!(a.contains(98));
[1627](https://docs.rs#1627)        assert!(a.contains(3));
[1628](https://docs.rs#1628)
[1629](https://docs.rs#1629)        a.shrink_to_fit();
[1630](https://docs.rs#1630)        assert!(!a.contains(1));
[1631](https://docs.rs#1631)        assert!(a.contains(259));
[1632](https://docs.rs#1632)        assert!(a.contains(98));
[1633](https://docs.rs#1633)        assert!(a.contains(3));
[1634](https://docs.rs#1634)        assert_eq!(a.count(), 3);
[1635](https://docs.rs#1635)        assert!(a.capacity() > 0);
[1636](https://docs.rs#1636)
[1637](https://docs.rs#1637)        let old_cap = a.capacity();
[1638](https://docs.rs#1638)        assert!(a.remove(259));
[1639](https://docs.rs#1639)        a.shrink_to_fit();
[1640](https://docs.rs#1640)        assert!(a.capacity() < old_cap, "{} {}", a.capacity(), old_cap);
[1641](https://docs.rs#1641)        assert!(!a.contains(1));
[1642](https://docs.rs#1642)        assert!(!a.contains(259));
[1643](https://docs.rs#1643)        assert!(a.contains(98));
[1644](https://docs.rs#1644)        assert!(a.contains(3));
[1645](https://docs.rs#1645)        assert_eq!(a.count(), 2);
[1646](https://docs.rs#1646)
[1647](https://docs.rs#1647)        let old_cap2 = a.capacity();
[1648](https://docs.rs#1648)        a.make_empty();
[1649](https://docs.rs#1649)        assert_eq!(a.capacity(), old_cap2);
[1650](https://docs.rs#1650)        assert_eq!(a.count(), 0);
[1651](https://docs.rs#1651)        assert!(!a.contains(1));
[1652](https://docs.rs#1652)        assert!(!a.contains(259));
[1653](https://docs.rs#1653)        assert!(!a.contains(98));
[1654](https://docs.rs#1654)        assert!(!a.contains(3));
[1655](https://docs.rs#1655)
[1656](https://docs.rs#1656)        a.insert(512);
[1657](https://docs.rs#1657)        assert!(a.capacity() > 0);
[1658](https://docs.rs#1658)        assert_eq!(a.count(), 1);
[1659](https://docs.rs#1659)        assert!(a.contains(512));
[1660](https://docs.rs#1660)        assert!(!a.contains(1));
[1661](https://docs.rs#1661)        assert!(!a.contains(259));
[1662](https://docs.rs#1662)        assert!(!a.contains(98));
[1663](https://docs.rs#1663)        assert!(!a.contains(3));
[1664](https://docs.rs#1664)
[1665](https://docs.rs#1665)        a.remove(512);
[1666](https://docs.rs#1666)        a.shrink_to_fit();
[1667](https://docs.rs#1667)        assert_eq!(a.capacity(), 0);
[1668](https://docs.rs#1668)        assert_eq!(a.count(), 0);
[1669](https://docs.rs#1669)        assert!(!a.contains(512));
[1670](https://docs.rs#1670)        assert!(!a.contains(1));
[1671](https://docs.rs#1671)        assert!(!a.contains(259));
[1672](https://docs.rs#1672)        assert!(!a.contains(98));
[1673](https://docs.rs#1673)        assert!(!a.contains(3));
[1674](https://docs.rs#1674)        assert!(!a.contains(0));
[1675](https://docs.rs#1675)    }

[1711](https://docs.rs#1711)    #[test]
[1712](https://docs.rs#1712)    fn test_truncate() {
[1713](https://docs.rs#1713)        let bytes = [0xFF, 0xFF, 0xFF, 0xFF, 0xFF, 0xFF];
[1714](https://docs.rs#1714)
[1715](https://docs.rs#1715)        let mut s = BitSet::from_bytes(&bytes);
[1716](https://docs.rs#1716)        s.truncate(5 * 8);
[1717](https://docs.rs#1717)
[1718](https://docs.rs#1718)        assert_eq!(s, BitSet::from_bytes(&bytes[..5]));
[1719](https://docs.rs#1719)        assert_eq!(s.count(), 5 * 8);
[1720](https://docs.rs#1720)        s.truncate(4 * 8);
[1721](https://docs.rs#1721)        assert_eq!(s, BitSet::from_bytes(&bytes[..4]));
[1722](https://docs.rs#1722)        assert_eq!(s.count(), 4 * 8);
[1723](https://docs.rs#1723)        // Truncating to a size > s.len() should be a noop
[1724](https://docs.rs#1724)        s.truncate(5 * 8);
[1725](https://docs.rs#1725)        assert_eq!(s, BitSet::from_bytes(&bytes[..4]));
[1726](https://docs.rs#1726)        assert_eq!(s.count(), 4 * 8);
[1727](https://docs.rs#1727)        s.truncate(8);
[1728](https://docs.rs#1728)        assert_eq!(s, BitSet::from_bytes(&bytes[..1]));
[1729](https://docs.rs#1729)        assert_eq!(s.count(), 8);
[1730](https://docs.rs#1730)        s.truncate(0);
[1731](https://docs.rs#1731)        assert_eq!(s, BitSet::from_bytes(&[]));
[1732](https://docs.rs#1732)        assert_eq!(s.count(), 0);
[1733](https://docs.rs#1733)    }

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/bit_set/lib.rs.html#356-361)

#### pub fn [reserve_len](https://docs.rs#method.reserve_len)(&mut self, len: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html))

Reserves capacity for the given `BitSet` to contain `len` distinct elements. In the case
of `BitSet` this means reallocations will not occur as long as all inserted elements
are less than `len`.

The collection may reserve more space to avoid frequent reallocations.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-7)Examples

```
use bit_set::BitSet;
let mut s = BitSet::new();
s.reserve_len(10);
assert!(s.capacity() >= 10);
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/bit_set/lib.rs.html#381-386)#### pub fn [reserve_len_exact](https://docs.rs#method.reserve_len_exact)(&mut self, len: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html))

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/bit_set/lib.rs.html#381-386)

#### pub fn [reserve_len_exact](https://docs.rs#method.reserve_len_exact)(&mut self, len: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html))

Reserves the minimum capacity for the given `BitSet` to contain `len` distinct elements.
In the case of `BitSet` this means reallocations will not occur as long as all inserted
elements are less than `len`.

Note that the allocator may give the collection more space than it requests. Therefore
capacity can not be relied upon to be precisely minimal. Prefer `reserve_len` if future
insertions are expected.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-8)Examples

```
use bit_set::BitSet;
let mut s = BitSet::new();
s.reserve_len_exact(10);
assert!(s.capacity() >= 10);
```

#### pub fn [shrink_to_fit](https://docs.rs#method.shrink_to_fit)(&mut self)

Truncates the underlying vector to the least length required.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-12)Examples

```
use bit_set::BitSet;
let mut s = BitSet::new();
s.insert(3231);
s.remove(3231);
// Internal storage will probably be bigger than necessary
println!("old capacity: {}", s.capacity());
assert!(s.capacity() >= 3231);
// Now should be smaller
s.shrink_to_fit();
println!("new capacity: {}", s.capacity());
```

# bit_set - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bit-set/latest/aarch64-apple-darwin/bit_set/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#description)Description

An implementation of a set using a bit vector as an underlying representation for holding unsigned numerical elements.

It should also be noted that the amount of storage necessary for holding a
set of objects is proportional to the maximum of the objects when viewed
as a `usize`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use bit_set::BitSet;
// It's a regular set
let mut s = BitSet::new();
s.insert(0);
s.insert(3);
s.insert(7);
s.remove(7);
if !s.contains(7) {
    println!("There is no 7");
}
// Can initialize from a `BitVec`
let other = BitSet::from_bytes(&[0b11010000]);
s.union_with(&other);
// Print 0, 1, 3 in some order
for x in s.iter() {
    println!("{}", x);
}
// Can convert back to a `BitVec`
let bv = s.into_bit_vec();
assert!(bv[3]);
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [BitSet](https://docs.rs/struct.BitSet.html)

- [Intersection](https://docs.rs/struct.Intersection.html)

- [Symmetric](https://docs.rs/struct.SymmetricDifference.html)- Difference
- [Union](https://docs.rs/struct.Union.html)

# bit-vec 0.9.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/bit-vec/^0.9.1

## Usage

Add this to your Cargo.toml:

```
[]
 = "0.9"
```
If you want [serde](https://github.com/serde-rs/serde) support, include the feature like this:

```
[]
 = {  = "0.9",  = ["serde"] }
```
If you want to use bit-vec in a program that has `#![no_std]`, just drop default features:

```
[]
 = {  = "0.9",  = false }
```
If you want to use serde with the alloc crate instead of std, just use the `serde_no_std` feature:

```
[]
 = {  = "0.9",  = false,  = ["serde", "serde_no_std"] }
```
If you want [borsh-rs](https://github.com/near/borsh-rs) support, include it like this:

```
[]
 = {  = "0.9",  = ["borsh"] }
```
Other available serialization libraries can be enabled with the
[ miniserde](https://github.com/dtolnay/miniserde) and

[features.](https://github.com/not-fl3/nanoserde)

`nanoserde`### Description

Dynamic collections implemented with compact bit vectors.

### Examples

This is a simple example of the [Sieve of Eratosthenes](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sieve_of_Eratosthenes)
which calculates prime numbers up to a given limit.

```
use BitVec;
let max_prime = 10000;
// Store the primes as a BitVec
let primes = ;
// Simple primality tests below our max bound
let print_primes = 20;
print!;
for x in 0..print_primes
println!;
let num_primes = primes.iter.filter.count;
println!;
assert_eq!;
```

# borsh 1.7.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/borsh/^1.6.0

**borsh-rs** is Rust implementation of the [Borsh](https://borsh.io) binary serialization format.

Borsh stands for *Binary Object Representation Serializer for Hashing*. It is meant to be used in
security-critical projects as it prioritizes [consistency, safety, speed](https://borsh.io), and comes with a
strict [specification](https://github.com/near/borsh#specification).

## Example

```
use ;
```
## Docs shortcuts

Following pages are highlighted here just to give reader a chance at learning that they exist.

## Advanced examples

Some of the less trivial examples are present in [examples](https://docs.rs/borsh/examples) folder:

## Testing

Integration tests should generally be preferred to unit ones. Root module of integration tests of `borsh` crate is [linked](https://docs.rs/borsh/tests/tests.rs) here.

## Releasing

The versions of all public crates in this repository are collectively managed by a single version in the [workspace manifest](https://github.com/near/borsh-rs/blob/master/Cargo.toml).

So, to publish a new version of all the crates, you can do so by simply bumping that to the next "patch" version and submit a PR.

We have CI Infrastructure put in place to automate the process of publishing all crates once a version change has merged into master.

However, before you release, make sure the [CHANGELOG](https://docs.rs/CHANGELOG.md) is up to date and that the `[Unreleased]` section is present but empty.

# rand 0.9.4 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rand/^0.9

# Rand

Rand is a set of crates supporting (pseudo-)random generators:

- Built over a standard RNG trait: `rand_core::RngCore`
- With fast implementations of both [strong](https://rust-random.github.io/book/guide-rngs.html#cryptographically-secure-pseudo-random-number-generators-csprngs)and[small](https://rust-random.github.io/book/guide-rngs.html#basic-pseudo-random-number-generators-prngs)generators:`rand::rngs``rand_chacha``rand_xoshiro``rand_pcg`[rngs repo](https://github.com/rust-random/rngs/)
- `rand::rng`- `std`targets
- Direct support for seeding generators from the [getrandom](https://crates.io/crates/getrandom)crate

With broad support for random value generation and random processes:

- `StandardUniform`- `Uniform`- [more](https://docs.rs/rand/latest/rand/distr/index.html)
- Samplers for a large number of non-uniform random number distributions via our own
`rand_distr``statrs`
- Random processes (mostly choose and shuffle) via `rand::seq`

All with:

- [Portably reproducible output](https://rust-random.github.io/book/portability.html)
- `#[no_std]`compatibility (partial)
- *Many*performance optimisations thanks to contributions from the wide user-base

Rand **is not**:

- Small (LoC). Most low-level crates are small, but the higher-level `rand`and`rand_distr`each contain a lot of functionality.
- Simple (implementation). We have a strong focus on correctness, speed and flexibility, but
not simplicity. If you prefer a small-and-simple library, there are
alternatives including [fastrand](https://crates.io/crates/fastrand)and[oorandom](https://crates.io/crates/oorandom).
- Primarily a cryptographic library. `rand`does provide some generators which aim to support unpredictable value generation under certain constraints; see[SECURITY.md](https://github.com/rust-random/rand/blob/master/SECURITY.md)for details. Users are expected to determine for themselves whether`rand`'s functionality meets their own security requirements.

Documentation:

## Versions

Rand is *mature* (suitable for general usage, with infrequent breaking releases
which minimise breakage) but not yet at 1.0. Current `MAJOR.MINOR` versions are:

- Version 0.9 was released in January 2025.

See the [CHANGELOG](https://github.com/rust-random/rand/blob/master/CHANGELOG.md) or [Upgrade Guide](https://rust-random.github.io/book/update.html) for more details.

## Crate Features

Rand is built with these features enabled by default:

- `std`enables functionality dependent on the- `std`lib
- `alloc`(implied by- `std`) enables functionality requiring an allocator
- `os_rng`(implied by- `std`) enables- `rngs::OsRng`, using the- [getrandom](https://crates.io/crates/getrandom)crate
- `std_rng`enables inclusion of- `StdRng`,- `ThreadRng`
- `small_rng`enables inclusion of the- `SmallRng`PRNG

Additionally, these features configure Rand:

-
`nightly`includes some additions requiring nightly Rust
-
`simd_support`(experimental) enables sampling of SIMD values (uniformly random SIMD integers and floats), requiring nightly Rust
-
`unbiased`use unbiased sampling for algorithms supporting this option: Uniform distribution.(By default, bias affecting no more than one in 2^48 samples is accepted.) Note: enabling this option is expected to affect reproducibility of results.

Note that nightly features are not stable and therefore not all library and
compiler versions will be compatible. This is especially true of Rand's
experimental `simd_support` feature.

Rand supports limited functionality in `no_std` mode (enabled via
`default-features = false`). In this case, `OsRng` and `from_os_rng` are
unavailable (unless `os_rng` is enabled), large parts of `seq` are
unavailable (unless `alloc` is enabled), and `ThreadRng` is unavailable.

## Portability and platform support

Many (but not all) algorithms are intended to have reproducible output. Read more in the book: [Portability](https://rust-random.github.io/book/portability.html).

The Rand library supports a variety of CPU architectures. Platform integration is outsourced to [getrandom](https://crates.io/crates/getrandom).

### WebAssembly support

The [WASI](https://github.com/WebAssembly/WASI/tree/main) and Emscripten
targets are directly supported. The `wasm32-unknown-unknown` target is not
*automatically* supported. To enable support for this target, refer to the
[ getrandom documentation for WebAssembly](https://docs.rs/getrandom/latest/getrandom/#webassembly-support).
Alternatively, the

`os_rng` feature may be disabled.# License

Rand is distributed under the terms of both the MIT license and the Apache License (Version 2.0).

See [LICENSE-APACHE](https://github.com/rust-random/rand/blob/master/LICENSE-APACHE) and [LICENSE-MIT](https://github.com/rust-random/rand/blob/master/LICENSE-MIT), and
[COPYRIGHT](https://github.com/rust-random/rand/blob/master/COPYRIGHT) for details.
